prompt:
You are a senior information designer and editorial typographer who sets data tables for high-quality publications (statistical yearbooks, reference works, financial reports, technical documentation) in many writing systems, including Chinese. You judge by looking at the real rendered result.

Judge a table layout on all of these levels, in this order of necessity but as one whole:
1. correctness — every character visible, structure intact, nothing clipped or overlapping;
2. readability — natural line breaks, words/numbers/identifiers/semantic units kept whole, continuous reading;
3. function — easy to look up, compare, locate and understand the information for this table's real reading tasks;
4. visual order — alignment, grouping, hierarchy, consistent scale for elements with the same role;
5. visual rhythm — proportion, density changes, distribution of white space, spatial relationships;
6. overall aesthetics — balance, restraint, naturalness, harmony.
Do not assume that equal widths, symmetry, minimum height, the fewest lines, the golden ratio or any fixed proportion is good in itself; decide from this table's function, content and reading task, and look for counter-examples to your own rules.

Table: UAX #14 Table 1. Line Breaking Classes (excerpt) (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 17 rows. Row headers: yes.
Merged cells: "Non-tailorable Line Brea" spans 4 col × 1 row; "Break Opportunities" spans 4 col × 1 row.
Measured content facts (text px at 15px font, padding excluded):
  col 1: header "Class" · longest unbreakable unit 40px · widest one-line content 40px
  col 2: header "Descriptive Name" · longest unbreakable unit 83px · widest one-line content 242px
  col 3: header "Examples" · longest unbreakable unit 89px · widest one-line content 308px
  col 4: header "Behavior" · longest unbreakable unit 80px · widest one-line content 492px
Each column adds 21px of padding+border to its text width.
Viewport: 720px wide (dashed pink box in the renders). The column widths must sum to at most 719px: the table must fit; no horizontal scrolling.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. Only the column widths are designed; row heights follow from them.

Your understanding: {"purpose":"Provide a compact reference to Unicode line-breaking classes, their names, examples, and behavior.","tasks":["Look up a class abbreviation and read across to its meaning, examples, and behavior.","Compare related classes, especially where their break behavior differs.","Scan each section sequentially to understand the range of classes."],"relations":["Each class code identifies a named class; its examples illustrate the characters covered, and its behavior describes the line-breaking effect.","The full-width section labels group classes by their role in line breaking."],"roles":["Class is the row header and primary lookup key; it needs little width but must remain easy to scan.","Descriptive Name translates the abbreviation into a recognizable concept.","Examples connects the class to characters or character categories.","Behavior carries the explanatory prose and is central to comparison.","Column headers label the fields; section rows separate the two groups."],"keep_whole":["Class abbreviations and other short identifiers such as ZWSP, NBSP, and ZWNBSP.","Individual words and numeric or technical identifiers.","Short names and examples where space permits."],"may_wrap":["Long descriptive names at word boundaries.","Example lists between items or words.","Behavior descriptions at natural word boundaries.","The Descriptive Name header if the column is narrow."],"same_scale":["All class codes should have a consistent narrow field.","Names, examples, and behaviors should remain readable as peer fields, while their widths reflect their different content lengths.","Both section labels should read as full-width group headings."],"h_vs_v":"The 719px limit requires wrapping: extra width for behavior reduces prose line breaks, while extra width for names or examples improves scanning and comparison in those fields. More wrapping increases row height, but can be preferable to fragmenting meaningful phrases or making the reference difficult to scan."}

Image 1 is the one-line content overview. Then real browser renders of: d1r4B, d1r1A.
Measured facts:
d1r4B: column widths [61, 170, 200, 288] px · table 720×803 px · row heights [36, 36, 60, 60, 36, 60, 36, 36, 36, 36, 60, 36, 60, 36, 60, 60, 60] · column headers on >1 line: 0/4 · tallest cell 2 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 0
d1r1A: column widths [61, 180, 190, 288] px · table 720×780 px · row heights [36, 36, 60, 60, 36, 60, 36, 36, 36, 36, 36, 36, 60, 36, 60, 60, 60] · column headers on >1 line: 0/4 · tallest cell 2 lines · measured breaks inside a word: 0

Look at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design: what works, what is visually wrong, and the cause (which width). Then either propose up to 3 improved designs (refine the most promising, fix what you saw, or try an important unexplored idea) or, if further changes would not bring a meaningful improvement, set "done": true. Do not resubmit near-identical widths.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"best":["your best design name(s) so far"],"done":false,"designs":[{"widths":[int px],"change":"what and why"}]}
